Chapter 3: The High Cost of Loyalty and the Strain on Family
Loyalty—it's something we often celebrate, especially when it comes to family or those tight circles we trust most. But what happens when loyalty isn't a gift, but a demand? When it starts to feel less like a virtue, and more like a weight you can’t put down?
In Scientology, loyalty to the church wasn't just encouraged—it took over everything else, even the bonds between family members. Imagine living in a world where the church’s influence doesn’t stop at the door; it seeps into every conversation, every relationship, and even your private thoughts.
There were rules about who you could trust, who you could talk to, and even what you could share. And get this—if you disagreed with someone in your family, it wasn’t just a personal issue anymore. Suddenly, it became church business, subject to scrutiny and intervention. Instead of working things out quietly at the kitchen table, families were often told to turn to church officials.
Now, imagine a family already dealing with its own ups and downs. For them, these pressures were magnified. The mother’s devotion to the church was total—any question or doubt was met, not with understanding, but with suspicion. Relatives, siblings, everyone got pulled into this web of expectations and rules—rules that, to anyone outside the church, would seem almost impossible to follow.
And then there’s the church’s policy of “disconnection.” If someone was seen as a threat to the church, members were expected to cut all ties—even with their closest family. That fear—of losing your loved ones, of ending up alone—kept people in line. Loyalty wasn’t just a value here; it was enforced, with real consequences.
Living in this environment meant secrecy and mistrust became the norm. Open, honest conversations? Those became rare. Instead, every word was weighed, every sentence carefully considered—because one wrong move could mean heartbreak. People wanted to protect their families, but they were caught between that love and the rules they’d been taught to follow. It was like always walking on eggshells.
But even in the middle of all that tension, family bonds found a way to survive. There were moments—small but meaningful—of laughter, of shared struggle, of quietly pushing back against the rules. The love between mother and daughter, between siblings, was real. It just had to work a little harder to shine through.
Over time, though, the cost of this loyalty became impossible to ignore. The church demanded everything—time, money, relationships—and somehow, it was never enough. The more you gave, the more was expected. Slowly, the realization started to sink in: true loyalty should be a choice, not an obligation. It’s meant to bring us together, not tear us apart.
Most of us never have to choose between our family and our beliefs. But for folks caught up in high-demand groups like this, that choice is painfully real. And the pain? It can linger for years, long after the decision is made.
